performers: Beatrice Harrison, cello; Symphony Orchestra; Edward Elgar, conductor
intro: Beatrice Harrison plays with Elgar conducting, barely two months after the concerto’s première. Their four acoustic record sides condense the work into sixteen minutes, from the cello’s opening declaration to the impatient finale.

sections.label: A · First side: recitative and lament
sections.mNote: The cello’s chords lead to the swaying E-minor tune

sections.label: B · Second side: the darting scherzo
sections.mNote: Plucked chords and fast, lightly bowed notes

sections.label: C · Third side: the Adagio
sections.mNote: A long cello melody in B♭ major

sections.label: D · Fourth side: the shortened finale
sections.mNote: The cello’s resolute tune meets brisk orchestral replies

cues.title: Harrison’s opening declaration
cues.text: Four insistent cello chords open the concerto. The orchestra answers quietly, and the soloist replies as though speaking. Soon the violas introduce the swaying E-minor tune that the cello takes over and carries through the movement.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 1, opening and rehearsals 1–2. The orchestral reply and viola melody are described by Frank Beck: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune from a nursing home
cues.text: In March 1918 Elgar has his tonsils out in a London nursing home. His daughter Carice remembers that he “woke up one morning and asked for pencil and paper and wrote down the opening theme of the Cello Concerto”: the swaying 9/8 melody of the violas.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”, quoting Carice Elgar Blake; the 9/8 melody as the concerto’s original impetus in Beck’s “A Musical Tour”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm and https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm

cues.title: Salmond at Queen’s Hall
cues.text: Felix Salmond gives the première on 27 October 1919 at Queen’s Hall. Elgar conducts the London Symphony Orchestra after too little rehearsal. Harrison takes the new concerto into the recording studio that December, with its composer again on the podium.
cues.evidence: Première and rehearsal circumstances: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Harrison’s first session, 22 December 1919: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: Playing it through at Brinkwells
cues.text: On 2 June 1919, Elgar’s sixty-second birthday, the conductor Landon Ronald visits Brinkwells and hears long passages of the concerto on the piano. Three days later the cellist Felix Salmond tries it on his cello. Alice writes in her diary: “FS most delighted and enthusiastic.”
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”, drawing on Alice Elgar’s diary: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Alice posts the score
cues.text: On 8 August 1919 Alice takes the completed concerto to Fittleworth Post Office and sends it to London. Elgar has spent the summer working at Brinkwells, often rising at four or five in the morning to score it and add new passages.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck’s composition history, drawing on Alice’s diary and the correspondence: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Plucked chords, flying bow
cues.text: The scherzo begins with plucked cello chords and little trials of a quick tune. Once the Allegro molto is under way, the bow scarcely rests: semiquavers climb, turn and tumble through the solo part.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 4–7, rehearsals 18–33: pizzicato recitative, repeated trials of the quick figure and Allegro molto. The second record side is listed as Lento – Allegro molto in the archive description.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A nineteen-year-old in the cellos
cues.text: Among the London Symphony Orchestra players at the première on 27 October 1919 is a nineteen-year-old cellist, John Barbirolli. In 1965 he conducts the recording with Jacqueline du Pré that many hail as the definitive one.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Barbirolli in the LSO at the première and the 1965 du Pré recording: Warner Classics, Elgar: Cello Concerto, Sea Pictures, https://www.warnerclassics.com/release/elgar-du-pre

cues.title: Ernest Newman’s review
cues.text: The critic Ernest Newman begins his review of the première by complaining of a ragged performance. Then he turns to the music: “The work itself is lovely stuff, very simple … a fine spirit’s lifelong wistful brooding upon the loveliness of earth.”
cues.evidence: Ernest Newman’s review of the première, quoted in Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: An awful slaughter
cues.text: On 14 December 1919 Elgar sends Beatrice Harrison “the copy with the cuts for the Gramophone”: “I fear it is an awful slaughter but it is the best I can do.” After the session on 22 December he writes that “recording is rather an ordeal” and thanks her for her “beautiful playing”.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Beatrice Harrison, 14 December 1919 (42 Netherhall Gardens, Hampstead) and Tuesday [23 December 1919] (the Athenaeum): typed transcripts shown in the Museum of Music History exhibition on Beatrice Harrison, https://momh.org.uk/exhibitions/beatrice-harrison-1892-1965/ (image https://momh.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/Image-10.jpg, read). The first session on 22 December 1919 is in the archive item cited in the Salmond note; the second letter’s “yesterday” agrees. Elgar’s preference for Harrison as the concerto’s soloist: Science Museum Group, https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp169411/beatrice-harrison ; Julian Lloyd Webber, Elgar Society Journal, January 1993, pp. 8–9, https://www.elgarsociety.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/JOURNAL_1993.01.pdf . The earlier note’s claims that she studied the concerto with Elgar and played it at a Royal Philharmonic Society concert in November 1925 rested on Wikipedia alone and are not used.

cues.title: The Adagio’s long breath
cues.text: The cello sings in B♭ major, far from the concerto’s E minor. Elgar marks the melody molto espressivo. Small rises and falls join into an almost continuous line, with the orchestra leaving the soloist space to linger.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 8, rehearsals 34–41: Adagio in B♭ major, molto espressivo. Frank Beck discusses its linked phrases: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back to Hayes
cues.text: Harrison and Elgar return to Hayes on 16 November 1920 to record the slow-movement side used here. The other three sides come from December 1919. HMV issues the two discs in May and June 1921.
cues.evidence: Session dates, the later Adagio matrix HO 4607-AF and release months: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: “My ideal!”
cues.text: In 1883 Elgar hears Schumann in Leipzig and writes to a friend: “My ideal!” Thirty-six years later Frank Beck hears Schumannesque echoes in the Adagio, whose B♭-major melody runs from phrase to phrase without a seam.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — A Musical Tour”, on Elgar’s Leipzig visit and the Adagio: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm

cues.title: A finale in four minutes
cues.text: The last record side gives the finale four minutes. Its brisk E-minor tune keeps returning to the cello, with firm accents and short orchestral replies. Harrison and Elgar compress the movement heavily to fit the disc.
cues.evidence: The archive identifies the abridged finale and its four-minute side: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545. The accented main theme appears in the Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, rehearsal 44.

cues.title: The Colvins’ concerto
cues.text: The dedication names Sidney and Frances Colvin, friends of the Elgars. In late July 1919, with the work almost finished, Elgar writes to Sidney that it is “a real large work and I think good and alive”.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Sidney Colvin, late July 1919; dedication and letter quoted by Frank Beck: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Whistling on the Malvern Hills
cues.text: During his last illness, in 1933, Elgar hums the concerto’s opening theme to a friend and says: “If ever after I’m dead you hear someone whistling this tune on the Malvern Hills, don’t be alarmed. It’s only me.”
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Cello Concerto — Creating a Classic”: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

transitions.title: The bow becomes a plucking hand
transitions.from: A · First side: recitative and lament
transitions.to: B · Second side: the darting scherzo
transitions.how: The first movement ends with three plucked cello notes in E minor. The next movement answers with plucked chords, marked Lento, before the bow tests a quick semiquaver figure. Elgar writes attacca in the score; on these records the two movements occupy separate sides.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 3–4, rehearsals 17–18. The archive lists a four-minute first side followed by the second movement: https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

transitions.title: The fast bow begins to sing
transitions.from: B · Second side: the darting scherzo
transitions.how: The scherzo’s last running notes end in a few plucked strokes. On the third side, the cello begins the B♭-major Adagio with a rising, bowed phrase, marked molto espressivo. The orchestra accompanies a long melody after the scherzo’s bursts of semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 7–8, rehearsals 33–34. The first two recorded sides last 4:00 and 3:52 in the archive’s listing.

transitions.title: Back to the brisk finale
transitions.to: D · Fourth side: the shortened finale
transitions.how: The B♭-major Adagio ends with the cello slowing into a held note. The fourth side returns to the finale’s E-minor argument: accented cello phrases and brisk orchestral answers. Its main tune carries the marking Allegro ma non troppo, with risoluto in the solo part.
transitions.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, pp. 8–9, rehearsals 41 and 44. The archive places the finale after sides lasting 4:00, 3:52 and 3:58; its opening is abridged.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Beatrice Harrison (cello), Symphony Orchestra (orchestra, as on the labels), Edward Elgar (conductor)
fields.note: The archive quotes Moore on the ensemble’s New Symphony/Royal Albert Hall identity; the published credit follows the photographed labels rather than silently expanding their wording.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Four acoustic sides, one movement per side; the whole concerto is abridged.
fields.note: This is the abridged whole concerto, not the complete score or a sixteen-minute finale. The supplied stream already joins all four sides. Only a continuous early finale passage is aligned with the complete Skidmore finale; neither complete work durations nor omitted music are equated. The exact cuts and acoustic-session instrumental substitutions are not established, so no modern-score orchestra timeline is projected onto this recording.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The later session applies to replacement side three, HO 4607-AF. The finale, HO 4198-AF, belongs to the December 1919 session; the listen ID names the two-session recording rather than dating every side to 1920.

fields.note: The archive estimates A=435 Hz at 78 rpm for the earlier sides and A=430 Hz for side three before correction. This is not a verified original session tuning. No local concatenation or audio processing was performed.

fields.label: Composition rights

fields.note: The archive identifies Elgar’s dates as 1857–1934. This term calculation does not clear a later edition.

fields.value: United States public domain: recording first issued in 1921, before the 1926 cutoff.
fields.note: Programme rule 2. The item states May and June 1921 issues and cites contemporary reviews; its metadata and description contain no non-commercial licence. The eligibility is based on the issued sound recording, not the composition. No unrestricted modern restoration licence is invented.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
